messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Diplomat
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan is a 24-year-old South Asian man who works as a junior diplomat, currently stationed in Washington D.C. following a posting abroad that ended abruptly under circumstances that have since reorganised the entire architecture of his inner life. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 66, and he arrives at the intake appointment dressed in a loose, long-sleeved shirt despite the warmth of the season, sitting with his back to the wall and his eyes tracking the door at intervals throughout the session.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rohan was stationed at a diplomatic mission in a city that came under sustained military assault over the course of several days. He had been attending a formal reception at a colleague's residence when the first strikes landed several blocks away. The building shook. Glasses fell. And then, in the minutes that followed, a portion of the outer wall collapsed under secondary pressure, and Rohan found himself on the floor amid smoke, plaster dust, and the smell of burning — a dense, particulate odour that mixed with the spilled wine and spirits from the overturned table beside him. A man he did not recognise stumbled toward him through the debris, face bloodied, arms outstretched, and Rohan, unable to move, lay still until colleagues reached him. He was not gravely physically injured. That fact, he has since decided, is evidence of something damning about him rather than something fortunate.

In the weeks that followed evacuation, Rohan began to notice that certain things undid him without warning. The smell of alcohol — at a dinner, near a bar, even hand sanitiser with the wrong chemical note — would return him without transition to the floor of that residence, the dust in his throat, the man walking toward him. A car backfiring, a door slamming in an adjacent room, construction work three streets over: any sharp, percussive sound could produce the same violent displacement, the same certainty that it was happening again, that the walls were coming down. He found himself in those moments not remembering the event but inhabiting it, speaking from inside it, and then returning to the present disoriented and ashamed. What frightened him most in these episodes was not the fear itself but his inability to accept reassurance. When his partner, Priya, held him and told him he was safe, he could hear the words and find them meaningless — not because he doubted her sincerity, but because he had come to believe that safety was simply not a category that applied to him anymore.

He began to manage. He started running — long distances, at punishing hours, pushing past discomfort into exhaustion, then further. He began using cannabis most evenings, and occasionally something stronger when the nights were bad. He took to wearing long, layered clothing whenever he left the apartment, operating on the quiet logic that if he was not visible, he was less of a target. He stopped attending diplomatic receptions entirely, citing workload, and then stopped attending most social functions associated with his posting. His supervisor has noted his withdrawal in two informal conversations, and a formal performance review is pending. Priya has told him she feels she is losing him, and he has not known what to say, in part because he knows what happened but finds that when he tries to speak about it the words simply do not exist — there is the event, vivid and sensory and present, but no language that reaches it. He can sometimes smell the smoke and spilled spirits when he sits with the memory, but he cannot explain to anyone, including himself, what he experienced.

What has settled most heavily over these fourteen months is not any single symptom but a set of convictions that have quietly taken up residence. He is certain there is something about him — some quality he cannot name — that made him a person to whom this would happen. He has lost whatever faith he held in the coherence of the world and in the people who move through it. Strangers who approach him in ordinary situations — a colleague crossing a room, a server leaning over to take his order — produce a spike of alarm that he finds humiliating and cannot override. He does not believe the future contains much for him. It was Priya who finally said the word therapy aloud, and it was the look on her face when she said it that brought him here. What he is most afraid of is that nothing will change. What he is most hoping, tentatively and almost against his will, is that someone can help him find the words.
